title: Social trust is associated with stated neighborly help and willingness to follow a public request
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel survey on neighborhood connection and social trust

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew's American Trends Panel survey

know_all_or_most_neighbors.unit: percent saying they know all or most of their neighbors

comfortable_asking_neighbor_keys.unit: percent saying they have a neighbor they would feel comfortable asking to keep emergency keys

would_help_neighbor_mail_plants.unit: percent saying it is extremely or very likely they would bring in mail or water plants for an out-of-town neighbor

would_conserve_if_public_official_asked.unit: percent saying it is extremely or very likely they would conserve water or electricity if asked by a public official

would_bring_meal.unit: percent saying it is extremely or very likely they would bring a meal to a sick neighbor or friend

observations.method: Weighted descriptive survey estimates from Pew's American Trends Panel; the source uses the same survey to compare generalized social trust with stated neighborly and public-request behaviors.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are self-reported attitudes or stated likelihoods, not observed assistance or compliance. The cross-sectional design does not establish whether social trust causes these intentions, whether a request occurred, or whether action was adequate or sustained.
observations.subgroup: Respondents classified as trusters or distrusters by the question whether most people can be trusted; the source also reports neighborhood, regional, demographic, and political-similarity comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trust, willingness to help, and willingness to follow a public request may all reflect safety, resources, local experience, political orientation, or question framing. Stated willingness toward a public official is not institutional trust or later civic action.

denominator.unit: percent within respondents classified as trusters or distrusters

trusters_would_conserve_if_public_offici.unit: percent of trusters saying extremely or very likely

distrusters_would_conserve_if_public_off.unit: percent of distrusters saying extremely or very likely

trusters_would_help_neighbor_mail_plants.unit: percent of trusters saying extremely or very likely

distrusters_would_help_neighbor_mail_pla.unit: percent of distrusters saying extremely or very likely

observations.method: Same-survey conditional comparison of stated likelihoods by generalized social-trust classification.
observations.uncertainty: The contrasts are descriptive and do not provide a randomized exposure, temporal order, effect estimate, or observed behavior. The public page does not expose all subgroup cell counts or a linked follow-up.
observations.subgroup: Pew-defined trusters and distrusters within the American Trends Panel survey.
observations.counterinterpretation: The differences may reflect common causes such as neighborhood safety, resources, social norms, ideology, or prior experience with institutions; trusting people may also report all cooperative intentions more readily.

related_sources.claim: Pew explains the truster/distruster contrasts and their relationship to willingness to help or follow a public request.

boundary: This record closes only a same-survey association between generalized social trust and stated neighborly/public-request willingness. It does not establish social trust as a cause, observe actual compliance or assistance, measure institutional performance, or show later political action, recovery, or durable community capacity.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Pew neighborhood-connection page downloaded and hashed; related Pew trust article cross-checked for conditional contrasts.
